text: Lipschitz stability for identification of piecewise constant conductivity coefficient in parabolic equation from finitely many interior point measurements The fundamental solution of a divergence-form parabolic equation with a measurable, uniformly elliptic coefficient matrix satisfies a specific derivative estimate. The coefficient matrix is assumed to be Lipschitz continuous in the spatial variable. The constants in the estimate depend only on the ellipticity constant, the dimension, and the Lipschitz constant. Under given conditions, the unique solution to the parabolic equation with initial condition linear in x is Lipschitz continuous in both time and space. The Lipschitz constant depends on the slope parameter theta. This constant is given by a function kappa of theta, which is locally bounded. The result holds for all real values of theta. For a constant p between 1 and infinity, assume the coefficients a are continuous with specified moduli of continuity on different parts of the domain. For any f in L_p, there exists a unique strong solution u in the Sobolev space W^{1,2}_p to the given parabolic equation with zero Dirichlet boundary condition. The solution satisfies an estimate where its norm is bounded by a constant times the norm of f. The constant depends only on the dimension, p, the ellipticity constant, and the moduli of continuity. Under certain conditions on the functions A and H, a solution u to a parabolic equation with bounded initial data and a time derivative bounded below remains Lipschitz continuous in space. The Lipschitz constant depends on the spatial domain and parameters from the problem. It is expressed in terms of given constants and the bounds on the solution and its derivatives. The constant K_r is explicitly given and depends only on the dimension and a parameter m.

text: convergence of Gauss-Newton or Levenberg-Marquardt for nonlinear least squares parameter estimation with finitely many parameters and Gaussian noise, asymptotic efficiency attaining Cramer-Rao bound Maximum likelihood estimation achieves the lowest possible variance for parameter estimation when the noise is Gaussian. This optimality is defined by the Cramér-Rao lower bound. The bound represents the smallest achievable variance for an unbiased estimator. The weighted least squares estimates for parameters a and eta are asymptotically efficient. Their scaled estimation errors converge in distribution to normal random vectors. The asymptotic covariance matrices equal the Cramer-Rao lower bounds multiplied by the noise variance. This efficiency holds for both parameter vectors under the given conditions. The W-estimator for the Gaussian model has an asymptotic normal distribution. The mean and standard deviation estimators are asymptotically unbiased. text: The Gauss-Newton method converges locally and quadratically for solving inverse problems involving neural network operators. This holds when the initial parameter vector is sufficiently close to a solution. The operator is linear, bounded, and has trivial nullspace and dense range. The neural network is shallow and defined by an activation function. Let $L:{\tt X}= L^2(]0,1[^m) \to {\tt Y}$ be a linear, bounded operator with trivial nullspace and dense range. Moreover, let $F= L \circ \Psi $, where $\Psi : {\cal D}(\Psi ) \subseteq \mathds {R}^{(m+2){\tt {M}}} \to {\tt X}$ is a shallow neural network operator generated by an activation function $\sigma $. Let ${\vec p}^0 \in {\cal D}(\Psi )$ be the starting point of the Gauss-Newton iteration \autoref{eq:newton} and let ${\vec p}^\dagger \in {\cal D}(\Psi )$ be a solution of \autoref{eq:sol}, which satisfy \autoref{eq:h}. Then the Gauss-Newton iterations are locally, that is if ${\vec p}^0$ is sufficiently close to ${\vec p}^\dagger $, and quadratically converging.

text: Lipschitz stability for recovering piecewise constant conductivity coefficient in parabolic equation from finitely many interior point measurements The inverse Robin problem for parabolic equations is locally Lipschitz stable. If the solution is bounded below by a positive constant on the inner boundary over time, then the difference in solutions on the accessible boundary controls the difference in Robin coefficients. This holds for all coefficients in a neighborhood of a given coefficient. The stability constant depends on the lower bound and the neighborhood size. For a Lipschitz domain D, given functions a and b in class A1, and a positive bounded function f, the L2 norm of the difference between a and b is bounded by a constant times the H01 norm of the difference between their corresponding solutions raised to the power one-sixth. The constant depends on the domain, dimension, ellipticity parameters, and the lower bound of f. The inequality also involves a constant C0 from a prior definition. This result provides a stability estimate for the inverse problem of recovering coefficients from solutions. The theorem establishes a stability estimate for the difference between two conductivity functions in a domain. It bounds the L-infinity norm of their difference on an inner subdomain by a sum of boundary differences and solution differences raised to a fractional power. The constants depend on domain parameters, boundary data, and operator coefficients. Under analytic boundary and coefficient conditions, the estimate holds on the entire domain. The fundamental solution of a divergence-form parabolic equation with a measurable, uniformly elliptic coefficient matrix satisfies a specific derivative estimate. The coefficient matrix is assumed to be Lipschitz continuous in the spatial variable. The constants in the estimate depend only on the ellipticity constant, the dimension, and the Lipschitz constant.

title: Hybrid: learned initializer + few LM steps through forward model reaches near-CRB accuracy
text: A kernel-ridge initializer on raw sensor traces lands within the basin of attraction of the MLE (log-transformed k), and 10-15 bounded LM iterations through F then drive per-sample error to near the Cramér–Rao floor, giving val/test rel_l2 < 0.035 (floor ~0.0195; model-mismatch is zero since the forward model is the generator). Noise sigma=1e-3 is tiny, the parameter count is 4, and the Fisher condition number is only ~47, so the problem is locally well-conditioned; the remaining difficulty is nonconvexity/initialization. A data-driven initializer removes the multistart cost, LM refinement removes the learned-map bias. author: researcher-ml
title: Learned initializer + Gauss-Newton/LM refinement with posterior-mean estimator approaches the Cramér-Rao floor
text: A torch MLP trained on simulated data, with noise augmentation, gives a starting point inside the local convergence basin of bounded LM through the forward model for nearly every sample. A few LM iterations in log-k space, followed by importance-sampled posterior-mean estimation under the box prior, then bring val rel_l2 to <= 0.03. That is within about 1.5x of the CRB floor of 0.0195, and well below what either component achieves alone. The diagnostics say the problem is well-posed at this noise level. The median Fisher condition number is 46.6, and the CRB rel_l2 floor is about 0.0195, below the 0.05 target. So the limiting factor is the estimator, not the information in the data. A purely learned map with 3000 training samples will likely carry approximation bias on top of the noise floor. Pure multistart LM risks local minima and wastes budget on bad starts. A learned initializer removes the basin problem. LM then removes the approximation bias, because it uses the exact forward model. Because rel_l2 is a squared-error-type loss, the posterior mean (MMSE) should beat the mode for the poorly determined k1 and k4, especially near the box bounds where the MLE gets clipped. The log transform enforces positivity and makes the box-constrained geometry more uniform, since sensitivity to k scales roughly like 1/k. Forward-model evaluations and Jacobians are cheap enough to run about 15 LM iterations for each of 750 val samples (and later test samples) within roughly 120 worker-seconds. The MLP initializer error (expected rel_l2 of about 0.05–0.1) lies inside the Gauss-Newton convergence radius. The Jacobian has full column rank across the prior box, which the finite Fisher condition number at 32 draws suggests. The noise is truly i.i.d. Gaussian with sigma = 0.001, so least squares is the correct likelihood. Near the posterior mode, the Laplace approximation is a reasonable proposal for importance sampling.

A high chi^2 on a subset points to local minima, so more extra_starts are needed. Normal chi^2 with high error means the CRB estimate from 32 draws is optimistic, and the floor is near the prior bounds.

author: researcher-ml
title: A purely amortized MLP with log-target and noise augmentation reaches the 0.05 target without physics at inference
text: The inverse map from sensor time series to log k is smooth and low-dimensional: 4 parameters, a well-conditioned Fisher matrix, and noise of sigma = 0.001 against signals of order 0.1–1. Under that assumption, a torch MLP trained on 3000 simulated pairs, with standardized raw features, log-target regression and 3x noise augmentation, achieves val rel_l2 < 0.05. It is expected to be worse than the physics-refined hybrid by at least 25% relative, because finite-sample approximation bias adds to the noise floor. Inference cost matters. If an amortized map already meets the success criterion, physics refinement is optional. Two choices fit the physics. Regressing log k matches the scale invariance of sensitivity, since the solution depends on k through diffusion time scales and relative errors are what rel_l2 penalizes. Noise augmentation at the true sigma forces the network toward the conditional mean of the posterior, rather than overfitting to the noise realizations in 3000 samples. This tests a specific claim: the remaining gap to the CRB (0.0195) is approximation and sample-size error, not information loss. The map from observations to log k is smooth enough that 3000 samples in a 4-D parameter space (about 7–8 per axis on a grid) are sufficient for an MLP with noise augmentation. Standardization per feature does not drown informative early-time or low-amplitude sensor readings. Sensors at indices 5 and 35 near the Dirichlet ends have small amplitudes, which is relevant to k1 and k4. The val distribution matches the training prior: uniform on [0.5, 2]^4 with the same noise.

Also report per-parameter relative error: k1 and k4 errors should exceed k2 and k3 errors by roughly the CRB ratio (about 3x). If they do not, the network's errors are not noise-driven.

If both fail, the CRB estimate at 32 draws is unrepresentative, likely near the box edges, and posterior truncation should be studied.

author: researcher-experimental
title: Learned initializer + LM refinement reaches the Cramér–Rao regime; MMSE beats MLE on the weak parameters k1 and k4
text: A hybrid estimator gets val rel_l2 <= 0.035, within about 1.8x of the CRB floor of 0.0195. It uses a torch_mlp initializer trained on simulated (theta, noisy observation) pairs, followed by bounded Levenberg–Marquardt in log-k space through the exact forward model, with the posterior-mean estimator under the uniform box prior. The competing explanation is that the forward model given to LM differs from the one that generated the data (discretization or sensor-index mismatch). In that case LM refinement would not improve on the initializer, and residual chi^2 per datum would sit well above 1. The forward model is available and cheap: explicit FD with 40 nodes and 200 steps. The noise is known i.i.d. Gaussian with sigma = 1e-3. So the likelihood is exact, and only optimisation and prior handling matter. The diagnostics give a median Fisher condition number of about 47, which is well conditioned for four parameters. Only k1 and k4 have CRB relative std around 2%, because the sensors at indices 5 and 35 sit near the Dirichlet ends where the pulse arrives late and weakly. A learned initializer places LM in the basin of attraction, so we need few starts and the budget stays small. Posterior mean under the box prior should shrink the noisy k1 and k4 estimates near the bounds. That can lower expected squared error below the per-parameter CRB, since the CRB applies only to unbiased estimators. context.forward is the same simulator that generated the train, val and test data: same grid, dt, sensor indices and initial condition. Noise is additive i.i.d. N(0, 1e-3^2) with no bias or correlation, as stated in facts. The log-transform keeps the problem away from the positivity boundary, and the LM Jacobian is accurate. Twelve LM iterations from an MLP init (initial error about 5–10%) are enough to converge in a well-conditioned 4-D problem. Compute: per-sample LM over 750 val samples x about 12 iterations x (1 + 4 Jacobian columns) forward solves of a 40x200 explicit scheme fits in about 60–100 worker-seconds.

Also report the mean residual chi^2/(n_obs*sigma^2) at the LM solution. The hypothesis is falsified if any of the following holds: (a) hybrid val rel_l2 > 0.035; (b) the median residual chi^2 per datum is > 1.5, which would indicate forward-model mismatch rather than optimisation failure; (c) per-parameter empirical relative RMSE for k1 and k4 exceeds 2x the CRB values of 0.021 and 0.016.

The CRB is then optimistic because of nonlinearity or bound effects, and we should look at the per-parameter error vs |k - bound|. If chi^2 is much greater than 1, the simulator and the data generator disagree. That is a simulation-fidelity bug to diagnose, for example with sensor-index off-by-one or time-subsampling checks on one training sample with known theta. If the init-only MLP is already below 0.035, LM is not needed.

author: researcher-experimental
title: Control: a purely amortized learned inverse (no forward model at inference) stalls above the target because sensor geometry under-determines the end segments
text: The best amortized data-driven model will reach val rel_l2 of at least 1.4x the best hybrid. We expect this model to be a noise-augmented torch_mlp on log-k targets trained on the 3000 simulated samples, and it should land in the range 0.03–0.06. Its excess error will be concentrated in k1 and k4: their per-parameter relative RMSE ratio to the CRB will be at least twice that of k2 and k3. The competing explanation is that 3000 samples suffice to learn the near-linear inverse map in a 4-D parameter space. In that case the amortized model would match the hybrid within 20%, and the per-parameter CRB ratios would be uniform. This is the evaluation-design control for proposal 1. Without it we cannot attribute any gain to physics refinement rather than to a good regressor. From a measurement-design viewpoint, sensors 5 and 35 are near the cold Dirichlet ends, so k1 and k4 enter the data through small, late-time signals. Those signals are of order 10–100 sigma. A regressor trained with a squared loss on 3000 samples in a 4-D input space has limited resolution for these weak directions. Its error is roughly approximation plus estimation error, which grows where the inverse map is most nonlinear and the SNR is lowest. Training with on-the-fly noise augmentation at the true sigma matches the train and test noise distribution. That removes one confound: overfitting to the specific noise realisations in the training set. The train, val and test features include noise at sigma = 1e-3 drawn from the same distribution. Noise augmentation at noise_scale=0.001 adds fresh draws and does not double the effective noise; if the harness adds noise on top of already-noisy features, the effective sigma rises by about 1.41x, which would bias this arm pessimistically, and this must be checked. The prior is uniform i.i.d. on [0.5, 2], so train and val cover the same theta distribution and there is no covariate shift. The log target transform makes the map from data to log k closer to linear and equalises relative errors across the range.
